units.t: The Nature of Life and Scientific Inquiry

lessons.t: Biology and the Characteristics of Life
learn: Biology is the study of life. All living things are made of cells, reproduce, have DNA, grow and develop, obtain and use energy, respond to their environment, maintain homeostasis and, as groups, evolve.
Viruses are a borderline case: they have genetic material but cannot reproduce without a host cell.
Biology connects to chemistry, physics, medicine and ecology.
check: Which is a characteristic of all life?
lessons.try: Argue whether a virus should be considered alive, using the characteristics.

learn: A controlled experiment changes one independent variable and measures a dependent variable.
A large sample size and repeated trials increase reliability.
A theory is a well-tested explanation supported by much evidence; a law describes what happens.
check: The variable you measure is the...
lessons.try: Design an experiment testing how light colour affects plant growth.

learn: Microscopes magnify specimens; total magnification = eyepiece × objective (10× × 40× = 400×).
Biologists use metric units and data tables.
Lab safety: goggles, gloves, no food, report accidents, handle living things humanely.
lessons.try: Calculate magnification for three microscope settings.

learn: Living things are mostly carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen.
Covalent bonds share electrons; ionic bonds transfer them; hydrogen bonds are weak attractions.
Water is polar, so it forms hydrogen bonds, giving it cohesion, high heat capacity and the ability to dissolve many substances.
lessons.try: Observe water beading on wax paper and explain cohesion.

learn: Carbohydrates provide energy (glucose, starch). Lipids store energy and form membranes.
Proteins are made of amino acids and do most of the cell's work. Nucleic acids (DNA, RNA) store genetic information.
Monomers link into polymers: amino acids into proteins, nucleotides into nucleic acids.
lessons.try: Make a chart of the four macromolecules with their monomers and functions.

learn: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions by lowering activation energy.
Each enzyme fits a specific substrate at its active site, like a lock and key.
Temperature and pH affect enzyme activity; too much heat denatures them.
check: Too much heat can ___ an enzyme.
lessons.try: Graph enzyme activity versus temperature from sample data.

learn: Prokaryotic cells (bacteria, archaea) lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi, protists) have a nucleus and organelles.
Prokaryotes are usually much smaller.
lessons.try: Draw and compare a bacterium and an animal cell.

learn: The nucleus stores DNA; ribosomes make proteins; the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus process and ship proteins.
Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration; chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.
Lysosomes break down waste; the cytoskeleton gives shape and movement.
lessons.try: Make an analogy comparing the cell to a factory.

learn: Robert Hooke named cells (1665); Anton van Leeuwenhoek saw living microbes.
Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow developed cell theory in the 1800s.
Electron microscopes reveal structures too small for light microscopes.
check: Who said all cells come from cells?
lessons.try: Make a timeline of cell theory discoveries.

learn: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins.
Phospholipids have hydrophilic (water-loving) heads and hydrophobic (water-fearing) tails.
The membrane is selectively permeable.
lessons.try: Draw the fluid mosaic model and label its parts.

learn: Diffusion moves particles down a concentration gradient.
Osmosis is diffusion of water; in a hypertonic solution cells shrink, in a hypotonic solution they swell.
Facilitated diffusion uses protein channels but no energy.
lessons.try: Predict what happens to a red blood cell in salt water.

learn: Active transport moves substances against a gradient using ATP.
The sodium-potassium pump maintains nerve cell function.
Endocytosis brings large particles in; exocytosis releases them.
lessons.try: Compare passive and active transport in a table.

learn: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) stores energy in its phosphate bonds.
Breaking off a phosphate releases energy, forming ADP.
Cells constantly recycle ATP.
check: Removing a phosphate from ATP forms...
lessons.try: Draw the ATP-ADP cycle.

learn: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
Light-dependent reactions in the thylakoids capture light energy and release oxygen.
The Calvin cycle in the stroma uses that energy to make glucose.
check: Oxygen is released during the ___ reactions.
The Calvin cycle occurs in the...
lessons.try: Diagram the two stages of photosynthesis.

learn: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP.
Glycolysis (cytoplasm), the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain (mitochondria) produce up to about 36-38 ATP per glucose.
Without oxygen, fermentation produces lactic acid or alcohol and much less ATP.
check: Aerobic respiration makes ___ ATP than fermentation.
lessons.try: Compare aerobic respiration and fermentation.

learn: DNA is a double helix of nucleotides: sugar, phosphate and a base (A, T, C, G).
Bases pair A-T and C-G.
Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images helped James Watson and Francis Crick describe the structure in 1953.
check: Whose X-ray images helped reveal DNA's structure?
lessons.try: Build a paper model of a DNA segment.

learn: Before cell division, DNA copies itself.
The helix unzips and each strand is a template for a new strand.
Replication is semi-conservative: each new DNA has one old and one new strand.
lessons.try: Write the complementary strand for ATGCCGTA.

learn: Transcription copies DNA into messenger RNA (mRNA) in the nucleus; RNA uses U instead of T.
Translation at ribosomes reads mRNA codons (three bases) to build proteins from amino acids.
Mutations change DNA sequences and can alter proteins.
lessons.try: Transcribe and translate a short DNA sequence using a codon chart.

learn: The cell cycle includes interphase (growth and DNA copying) and mitosis.
Checkpoints control the cycle; uncontrolled division can lead to cancer.
Most of a cell's life is spent in interphase.
lessons.try: Draw a pie chart of the cell cycle stages.

learn: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (PMAT), then cytokinesis.
Chromosomes line up in metaphase and separate in anaphase.
Mitosis produces two identical diploid cells for growth and repair.
lessons.try: Identify stages of mitosis in photographs.

learn: Meiosis makes four haploid gametes (sperm or eggs) with half the chromosomes.
Crossing over and independent assortment create genetic variety.
Fertilisation restores the diploid number: in humans, 46 chromosomes.
lessons.try: Compare mitosis and meiosis in a chart.

learn: Gregor Mendel's pea experiments showed traits are inherited as discrete units (genes).
Law of segregation: allele pairs separate in gametes. Law of independent assortment: genes for different traits sort independently.
Genotype is the alleles (Bb); phenotype is the trait (brown eyes).
check: Allele pairs separate in gametes is the law of...
lessons.try: Explain Mendel's results using a Punnett square.

learn: Bb × Bb gives 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, a 3:1 phenotype ratio.
A dihybrid cross (AaBb × AaBb) gives a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
A test cross with a recessive individual reveals an unknown genotype.
check: Bb × Bb gives a ___ phenotype ratio.
Bb × bb: probability of bb is...
lessons.try: Complete a dihybrid cross.

learn: Incomplete dominance blends traits (red × white = pink flowers).
Codominance shows both (AB blood type). Sex-linked traits are on the X chromosome, like colour blindness.
Many traits are polygenic (height, skin colour) and influenced by environment.
check: Pink from red and white is...
lessons.try: Analyse a pedigree for a sex-linked trait.

learn: Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection: variation, overproduction, competition and differential survival.
Fitness means reproductive success, not strength.
Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is natural selection we can observe.
check: Natural selection was proposed by Darwin and...
Antibiotic resistance is an example of...
lessons.try: Explain how antibiotic resistance evolves.

learn: Fossils, homologous structures, vestigial structures, embryology and DNA all support evolution.
Homologous structures share ancestry; analogous structures share function only.
Molecular similarities show relatedness between species.
check: A whale flipper and a human arm are...
lessons.try: Compare homologous and analogous structures with examples.

learn: Linnaean classification: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
Cladograms show evolutionary relationships based on shared traits.
check: The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and...
lessons.try: Build a cladogram for five animals.

learn: Energy flows from producers through consumers; about 10% passes to each level.
Matter cycles: carbon, nitrogen and water cycles.
Population growth can be exponential until it reaches carrying capacity (logistic).
check: About ___ of energy passes between levels.
The maximum population an environment supports is...
lessons.try: Graph a logistic growth curve and label carrying capacity.

learn: Habitat loss, pollution, invasive species, climate change and overharvesting threaten biodiversity.
Conservation, restoration and sustainable practices reduce harm.
Biodiversity provides food, medicine and ecosystem services.
check: A major threat to biodiversity is...
lessons.try: Research a conservation success story.

learn: Organ systems interact: nervous and endocrine systems control; circulatory and respiratory deliver oxygen; digestive and excretory process nutrients and waste.
Negative feedback maintains homeostasis, like regulating blood sugar with insulin.
The immune system defends against pathogens.
check: Hormones are part of the ___ system.
lessons.try: Diagram how the body regulates temperature.
